0.0.n: Names the first facial feature in a list; Japanese does not mark it as plural.

0.2.n: Names the second facial feature in the list.

0.4.n: Can also refer to the chin; here it names another surgically altered facial feature.

0.6.n: Refers collectively to the facial features just listed.

0.7.n: メスが入る describes undergoing surgery; the particle が is omitted in this casual sentence.

0.8.n: Short for 入っている, from 入る; with メス, it describes the lasting result of surgical intervention.

1.0.n: Contrasts unaltered body parts with those that have undergone cosmetic surgery.

1.1.n: Links 天然 to 場所, presenting naturalness as a quality of those parts.

1.2.n: Usually refers to a place, but here means areas of the person's face or body.

1.3.n: The plain form of 探す modifies 方; the object marker を after 場所 is omitted.

1.4.n: Read ほう here; it singles out finding natural parts as the harder alternative.

1.5.n: Marks the preceding activity as what is being described as difficult.

1.6.n: Means difficult; the comparison with finding surgically altered parts is implied by 方.

1.7.n: Short for の in んだ, giving the statement an explanatory or emphatic tone.

1.8.n: Combines with ん to form んだ, a casual explanatory ending.

1.9.n: At the sentence end, it leaves the thought hanging and adds a pointed, conversational tone.

0.lit: Eyes, nose, jaw—all have had a scalpel go in.
0.tip: メスが入る means to undergo surgery; casual speech drops が and shortens 入っている to 入ってる.

1.lit: Finding natural parts is the harder option, though.
1.tip: A verb followed by 方が難しい means doing that is harder, even when the alternative is left unstated.
